GLEUHR
Branch Leadership  •  The Branch Manager
Aesthetic Medicine
Branch Manager Playbook
Version 1.0   |   The Steady Hand the Branch Reaches Toward
The doctor holds the consultation.
The counsellor holds the plan.
The therapist holds the cabin.
The FDM holds the floor.
You hold the branch — the team that runs it, the patients who escalate to you, the numbers that report up, the standard that has to survive your absence.

This playbook is about how you hold all of that without holding it tightly.


The BM's Inner Stance
Read this before the branch opens. It takes one minute. It is the difference between a manager the team works for and a leader the team chooses every morning.
What the branch is actually carrying
Eight to twelve people. Each with their own pressure on a given day. A doctor who is fighting to keep clinical excellence under commercial weight. A counsellor whose conversion number is being watched at the head office. An FDM holding the floor through a busy afternoon. Therapists carrying their patients' confidences. A receptionist whose patience is tested by every angry caller. Housekeeping holding a standard no one acknowledges.
Each of them is doing real work. Each of them is reading the manager's mood within the first ninety seconds of the day. Each of them works fifteen percent harder for a leader they believe in than for a manager they tolerate. Your job is to be the first kind.
The boss trap
Branch managers in healthcare are often promoted because they were excellent in their previous role — the best counsellor, the best operations person, the best biller. The instinct is to keep performing the previous role from a new chair. That is not the job.
The job is to make every person in this branch better at their own role than they would be without you. That is not done by doing their work. It is done by setting direction, holding the standard, defusing what threatens them, and being the steady person they all reach toward when something tightens.
INNER STANCE  The branch should run when you are not in it. If it does not, you are not a manager — you are a single point of failure. The work of leadership is to build a team and a standard that holds in your absence. Your effectiveness is measured by what happens on the days you are not there. Aim for the branch that runs as well at 3 pm on your day off as it does at 11 am when you are in your chair.
Your three jobs as the BM
1.  Hold the standard. The branch operates at the GLEUHR standard — clinical, operational, commercial — every day, with or without you on site. You are the keeper of the standard, not the executor of it.
2.  Hold the team. Eight to twelve people, each with a life, each with a hard day every now and then. Notice them. Develop them. Defend them. Correct them privately. Praise them specifically. Retain them.
3.  Hold the brand. When something goes wrong, the patient asks for you. When the brand needs a real apology, it comes from you. When a complaint reaches HQ, it should already be on your desk. You are the face of GLEUHR for this branch.
The BM you should be
Picture the most respected school principal you ever knew. Not a stern one. The kind whose presence made the corridor walk straighter, whose praise was specific and rare enough to be cherished, whose correction was private and kind, whose office every staff member trusted but no one feared. Steady. Warm. Visibly competent. The kind of leader who is named in good stories years after she has moved on.
0.  The First Hour  —  Before the Branch Opens
Your day starts before everyone else's. The first hour is yours — to think, to walk, to brief, to set the tone.
Walk the branch in full, alone, before the team's morning. Look at it as a patient would. Note three to five things you will mention to the FDM or housekeeping after the huddle. Note one thing you will praise publicly.
Read yesterday's numbers. Footfall, conversion, walk-ins, complaints, follow-up calls owed. Do not just glance — actually read. If the FDM's debrief from yesterday is not in your inbox, ask why before 9 am.
Read today's appointment list. Mark the names that matter — VIPs, returning complaints, the patient who is on her fifth session and might be drifting, the new patient who came on a referral.
Look at the team roster. Anyone new, anyone returning from leave, anyone whose energy needs a check today.
Check the HQ inbox — anything from Manisha, Saurabh, Tejinder, Dr Kanikta, Urminder sir? Reply briefly to acknowledge, even if the full reply is going later in the day.
Plan your day in three buckets — patient-facing time, team time, paperwork. Block the patient-facing time first. Paperwork expands to fill any space; protect it last.
AVOID  Do not start the day in your inbox. Do not start the day on a phone call. Do not walk into the team huddle still mentally on yesterday's last problem. The team reads your morning before you have said hello — if you walk in tight, the floor is tight by lunch.
1.  The Morning with the Doctor  —  Same-Day MoM Rule
Every morning, ten to fifteen minutes with the senior doctor. The two of you running the branch — her on the clinical side, you on the operational and commercial side. The meeting is short, structured, and ends with the day aligned between two leaders.
The structure
Yesterday  —  in two sentences. ‘Yesterday we did 22 consults, 14 conversions, one mild reaction on Mrs Sharma in cabin 2, well-handled. Mrs Khanna returned for her second session, very pleased.’
Today  —  any patient that needs both of us paying attention. ‘Mrs Sharma is returning for her follow-up at 11 — please give her a few extra minutes. Mrs Mehta is in at 3 — she was wavering on her package last visit, the counsellor will need your weight in the room.’
Standards  —  one thing each is holding the other to this week. ‘We agreed last week the doctor handovers would slow down to give the counsellor more context. How is that landing for you?’
Anything stuck  —  one minute on anything that is not flowing. A therapist who needs sign-off on a new procedure. A consumable that has not arrived. A consult room that needs maintenance.
MoM  —  one note, three bullets max, sent to the same loop the same morning. Same-day rule. Anything that is not written down the same day did not happen.
FIRST AFFIRMATION  ·  THE MORNING WITH THE DOCTOR
“We run this branch together. Clinical is yours; operational is mine. The patient gets the best of both.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The doctor and the BM are the two leaders of the branch. When they are aligned and visibly so, the team operates with one direction; when they are not, the team feels the friction and the patients feel it after that. Fifteen minutes of structured morning time, every day, is the cheapest insurance against branch friction ever invented. Skip it under pressure and pay for it in the afternoon.
2.  The Branch Walk  —  What You Should See
Twice a day. Once mid-morning, once late afternoon. Twenty minutes each. The walk is the most important way you stay close to the actual experience of the branch — your patients' experience, your team's experience, your physical brand.
What you are looking at
Reception — is the desk clean, the receptionist warm, the phone being answered well, the water area stocked, the dustbin under?
Waiting area — do the patients look at ease? Is anyone waiting too long unattended?
Washroom — the hourly check signed, fresh, dry, stocked?
Corridor — quiet, ordered, no used-linen visible?
Cabins (between patients) — reset complete, trolley aligned, fragrance set?
Doctor's room — organised, file on her desk, no clutter?
Counsellor's room — calm, brochures current, no number visible from where the patient sits?
Team energy — who is up, who is down, who is moving slower than usual?
How you walk
Slowly. Visibly. Warmly. Greet every staff member you pass by name. Stop briefly at the desk and ask the receptionist how the morning is going. Look in on the counsellor between patients and ask her one specific thing. Catch the doctor between consults for thirty seconds. The walk should feel like a respected leader being present — not a regional manager inspecting.
Where the walk differs from the FDM's
The FDM walks for compliance — is the standard being held in detail. You walk for direction — is the standard the right one, is the patient experience what we want, is the team in the shape we need them in. Yours is a strategic walk; hers is a tactical one. Both are essential. Do not duplicate her work.
INNER STANCE  If you find yourself doing the FDM's walk, you are doing two things wrong — not letting her own her role, and not doing your own. Your walk is about whether the brand is showing up in this branch this morning. Hers is about whether the standard is being held. Different lenses. Different questions. Do yours; let her do hers.
3.  The Returning Patient  —  The Personal Greeting
Some patients should be greeted personally by the BM. Not all — most. Some. Choose deliberately.
Who
Long-standing patients on their fifth-plus visit — these are the people who refer.
Any patient flagged as VIP, by HQ or by referral chain.
Any patient returning after a previous complaint — this greeting is non-negotiable.
Any patient who has clearly come from outside the city — acknowledge the journey.
Any patient with a special occasion — birthday, anniversary, post-wedding follow-up.
What you say
“[Name]ji, what a pleasure to see you again. I just wanted to come and say a personal hello. Doctor mentioned your last session went beautifully — we are so glad. I hope today is just as good. If anything at all needs my attention, please ask the desk to find me directly.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The patient who is personally greeted by the manager goes home and tells someone. ‘The manager came out to say hello.’ That single sentence creates more referral lift than a month of marketing. It costs you ninety seconds. The patients who do not get the personal greeting are not lesser — the FDM and the receptionist are giving them the same warmth. But the ones who do get it should be chosen deliberately, and the gesture should be genuine.
4.  The Escalated Complaint  —  When the FDM Brings the Patient to You
A patient has crossed the FDM. Either by request — ‘I want to speak to the manager’ — or by judgment — the FDM has read the situation as one that needs you. Either way, the patient is now sitting across from you. The next ten minutes set the entire future of this relationship.
Before you start  —  brief yourself in twenty seconds
The FDM, who walked the patient to your room, gives you a one-sentence brief in the corridor. ‘Mrs Sharma, third session, unhappy with the result and the way she felt rushed by the counsellor today. Already given water, already moved off the floor.’ You walk in already knowing the contour. Now you can be present, not catching up.
What you do  —  in this exact order
Stand briefly when she walks in. Introduce yourself by name and role with warmth, not formality. ‘[Name]ji, I am [your name], the Branch Manager here. Thank you for waiting. Please sit — anywhere you'd like.’
Sit at her level, not behind a desk if the room allows. The desk is a barrier; a chair beside her removes it.
Open with appreciation. ‘Thank you for telling us this. Most people do not, and we never get the chance to fix it. I am very glad you have.’
Listen — fully. Even if the FDM has briefed you, let the patient tell you herself. Do not interrupt, do not defend, do not fill silences.
Acknowledge specifically. ‘What I am hearing is…’ Repeat back her concerns in your own words. Ask her to correct you if you have any of it wrong.
Apologise without litigating. ‘That should not have happened to you. I am sorry.’ Do not say ‘I'm sorry you feel that way’ — that is not an apology, it is a deflection. Apologise for the thing that happened.
Take responsibility, by name. ‘This is on me — not on the counsellor. The standards in this room are mine to hold. I missed something here, and I am sorry.’ The patient hears this and her body softens visibly.
Resolve, in a way she did not have to demand. Offer something concrete — a fresh consultation with the doctor today, a complimentary session, a refund where right, a manager-handled next visit. Decide based on what would genuinely make this right, not on what the policy minimum allows.
Commit to follow-through, with a timeline. ‘I will call you myself the day after tomorrow to check how you are feeling. If it is still not right, we will keep working on it.’
Document. Same hour. Into the file, the complaint log, and an email to the FDM and the doctor with the resolution. Copy Saurabh / HQ if it is material.
Make the call you promised. The follow-through is the real apology. Anything in this room can be undone by a missed callback.
What you say
“[Name]ji, I want to say two things clearly. One — what happened to you today is not the standard we want to deliver, and I am sorry. Two — this is mine to fix, not yours to chase. I am going to ask the doctor to come in personally in a moment, I am going to send you home with [the resolution], and I am going to call you myself on Thursday to make sure you are feeling better. Is there anything else, while you are here, that I should know?”
SECOND AFFIRMATION  ·  THE COMPLAINT
“This is mine to fix, not yours to chase. I am going to call you myself on Thursday.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  Most patients escalating to a manager are not asking for compensation. They are asking for ownership. ‘Someone with authority should hear this and own it.’ When the manager takes responsibility by name — ‘this is on me’ — the patient's nervous system relaxes in a way that no amount of compensation alone achieves. The compensation that follows then lands as care, not bribery. Reverse that order, and the same compensation feels like a payoff.
AVOID  Do not blame the counsellor or therapist by name in front of the patient — ever. ‘The counsellor will be spoken to’ is fine; ‘the counsellor was wrong’ humiliates the team and erodes the trust patients have in our staff. Do not promise something you have not decided you will deliver. Do not commit to a callback you will not make. Do not let the conversation end without a clear, concrete next step in her hand.
5.  The Refund or Dispute  —  When Money Is on the Table
Refund requests are the hardest commercial decision a BM makes. Each one is a balance of three things — what is right for this patient, what is right for the business, and what precedent is being set for the team.
How to think about it
If a refund is morally right, give it cleanly and warmly. Do not negotiate downward, do not delay, do not make the patient ask twice. The cost of a fair refund is small; the cost of a fair patient turned into a hostile one is years of revenue.
If a refund is not right — because services were rendered, because the patient changed her mind, because the package was used — say so with respect and offer a real alternative. ‘We cannot refund the sessions you have already received, and I would not feel right doing that. What I can do is freeze the remaining sessions — you can come back for them in six months, or pass them to a family member.’
Anything over a certain threshold needs HQ approval (per policy). Do not stretch the threshold yourself. Escalate cleanly, decide quickly, communicate to the patient with a clear timeline.
What you say  —  if you are saying yes
“[Name]ji, I have thought about this and I think you are right. We are going to process the refund for the [specific amount]. It will be back in your account within [X working days]. I am sorry it came to this, and I hope when you are ready, you will come back — a fresh consultation, no obligation. Whatever you decide, please call me directly if anything else comes up.”
What you say  —  if you are saying no
“[Name]ji, I want to be honest with you. I have looked at this carefully — the sessions you have received have been delivered as planned, and the costs we have incurred on them are real. I cannot refund those in good conscience. What I can do is [the alternative]. I know this is not what you were hoping to hear. I am genuinely sorry.”
INNER STANCE  The biggest mistake managers make on refunds is being slow. A slow refund is read as resistance, and the patient hardens. A fast refund — even one she did not expect — lands as integrity. Decide quickly. Communicate quickly. Process quickly. Speed is itself a form of respect.
6.  The Struggling Team Member  —  When Someone Is Not Carrying Their Role
Eventually, a team member is not performing. Conversions have slipped, customer feedback has dipped, attendance has wobbled, the FDM has flagged repeated small misses. You have two paths — develop or replace. Most of the time, the right answer is develop. Almost no one came into this work to be bad at it.
The development conversation
In private. Closed-door office, not the corridor.
Specific. Three concrete examples from the last two weeks, not vague ‘you have been off.’
Curious before corrective. ‘Help me understand what has been happening for you.’ Sometimes the answer is something none of us saw — a health issue, a family situation, a feeling of being passed over.
Co-author the path forward. ‘Here is what I am going to do to support you — [specific]. Here is what I am asking from you over the next four weeks — [specific]. We will sit again in two weeks.’
Write it down. A short one-page note. Sign it together. Not as a threat — as a shared commitment.
Tell HR / HQ briefly. They should not be surprised later.
If after a real development effort it is still not working
The replacement conversation is a separate moment, with the same care. By that point, the team member should not be surprised. If she is surprised, you skipped the development step. Do not skip it; do not let an underperformer leave thinking she never had a chance.
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The team member who is told the truth, kindly, and given a real path — either improves dramatically, or leaves on terms they themselves come to accept. The team member who is left to fail without intervention does damage in two directions — to the patients she serves badly, and to the colleagues who watch leadership fail to act. Holding the team is sometimes the hardest part of this role. Do not avoid it.
7.  Team Conflict  —  Doctor and Counsellor, Counsellor and FDM, Therapist and Therapist
Tension between team members will happen. The counsellor feels the doctor's handovers are rushed. The FDM feels the counsellor is too slow between patients. Two therapists are not speaking after a cabin disagreement. Conflict that is ignored becomes the culture of the branch. Conflict that is addressed becomes the team's growth.
What you do
Hear both sides separately, first. Never in the same room until you have heard each one alone.
Listen for the underlying need, not just the surface grievance. ‘The handover is rushed’ usually means ‘I feel set up to fail with this patient.’ ‘Sessions are slow between patients’ usually means ‘I am being held to a timing standard with no support.’
Bring them together, with you in the room, with a structured conversation. Each speaks. Each repeats back what the other said. You facilitate, you do not adjudicate.
Agree on one concrete change each will make. Write it down. Revisit in two weeks.
Do not pick sides publicly. Even when you privately think one side is more right.
INNER STANCE  The branch will read you on this one closely. The manager who picks sides creates a faction. The manager who avoids conflict creates a toxic peace. The manager who facilitates the hard conversation creates a team. The third option is the only correct one, and it is the hardest. Do it anyway.
8.  The Customer Who Wants to Escalate to HQ
Occasionally a patient will say ‘I want to speak to the owner’ or ‘I will be writing to your head office’ or ‘I am going to call the founder directly.’ The right move is the opposite of defending yourself or your team.
What you say
“[Name]ji, please do — you absolutely should, if it would help. Our HQ takes patient feedback seriously, and Urminder sir reads patient escalations himself. I want you to know that I will also be writing to them about this from my side, today, with everything we have done so far to address it. If they ask me for more information, I will share it openly. And whatever they decide is right, I will honour.”
Note what you have done. You have not tried to talk her out of escalating. You have not gone defensive. You have told her HQ will take her seriously, and that you yourself are writing to them. The patient who was bracing for a fight has just been disarmed by the opposite of resistance.
Then — actually write to HQ the same day
Saurabh, Manisha, and the BM's reporting line should hear from you before the patient's message reaches them. The facts as they happened. What you have done. What you are doing next. A line about your assessment. No spin. No defensiveness. If you made a mistake, name it.
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The patient escalating to HQ wants to feel that her complaint will not be swept under a rug. The manager who supports her escalation — and is visibly the one writing to HQ herself — removes the entire energy of the escalation. The patient is now part of the same loop as the manager, not in opposition to it. Almost no patient who is treated this way actually follows through to HQ aggressively. The few who do, do so calmly — and HQ already has your version.
9.  Decision Under Pressure  —  How to Decide When Time Is Short
There will be moments when the right answer is not clear, the clock is moving, and someone needs you to decide. Refund or not. Reschedule the patient or push her in today. Escalate the doctor's procedure question or wait for Dr Kanikta. Trust the receptionist's call on the angry caller, or step in.
The decision filter — three questions, in this order
Is this a clinical question? If yes, the doctor decides, not me. My job is to enable her to decide quickly.
Is this a brand question? If a wrong decision damages the brand more than the cost of doing the right thing — do the right thing, fast.
Is this within my authority and reversible? If yes, decide quickly, document, and move. If it is irreversible or outside my authority, escalate within the hour.
When you do not know
Say so. Out loud, to the team or to the patient. ‘I do not want to decide this in the next thirty seconds when there are real consequences. Give me ten minutes — I will be back with an answer.’ Honest pause beats wrong decision every single time.
AVOID  Do not make irreversible decisions under pressure to avoid looking indecisive. The cost of a ten-minute pause is small. The cost of a wrong refund, a wrong staff suspension, a wrong patient promise, a wrong escalation to HQ — is large. Calmness in slowing down is itself a leadership signal.
10.  End of Day with the Team  —  The Close
The day is winding down. The FDM is closing the floor. You step into the closing for the last ten minutes, every day you are on site.
What you do
Stand briefly with the team — by the desk, in the corridor, wherever they have gathered. Not a meeting. A presence.
Name two or three specifics from the day, by person. ‘Mrs Sharma's complaint today was handled beautifully by Jaspreet and the doctor — thank you, both. Suman, the way you read Mrs Mehta's hesitation and brought her back was excellent. Housekeeping kept the washroom checks tight today even when we were behind — thank you.’
Acknowledge anything hard. ‘Today was tough — we were behind from 10 and never quite caught up. You held the standard anyway. Thank you for that.’
Close warmly. ‘Have a good evening. Sleep well. See you tomorrow.’
THIRD AFFIRMATION  ·  THE TEAM CLOSE
“Thank you, team. Today was good because each of you held your part. Have a good evening.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The team that hears its name in the close stays. The team that does not, drifts. Every leader of a branch underestimates how much specific, public, daily acknowledgement matters — because it does not feel like work to give it. It is the most disproportionately leveraged thing a manager does all day.
Then  —  the manager's solo close
Read the FDM's debrief. Reply briefly, even with one line, the same evening.
Write your own short note to HQ if anything material happened — a complaint, a reaction, a refund, a staff issue. Same-day rule.
Make any patient callback you owe — the complaint follow-ups, the VIP thank-yous, the off-shift conversations. Most of these are best done in the early evening.
Walk the branch one last time, if you are last out. The condition you leave it in is the morning team's first impression tomorrow.
11.  Communication Rules  —  The BM Code
Always
Walk into the team huddle warm, not tight.
Meet the doctor every morning. MoM same day.
Walk the branch twice a day.
Greet returning patients personally — the ones who matter to the brand.
Take responsibility by name when something has gone wrong — never deflect to a team member in front of a patient.
Make every callback you promise.
Document complaints and escalations same day.
Close the day with the team, every day you are on site.
Name specifics in the close. Two or three a day.
Never
Never blame a team member by name in front of a patient.
Never correct a team member in the corridor or in front of others.
Never make a refund decision under pressure without thinking — take ten minutes if you need them.
Never let a patient walk out unhappy without owning it.
Never let HQ hear about a problem from the patient before they have heard about it from you.
Never make a clinical decision — the doctor decides clinical, always.
Never pick sides publicly in a team conflict.
Never go home with an undocumented complaint or an unmade callback.
Never raise your voice on the floor. Ever.
12.  The Goal of the BM  —  In Order of Importance
1.  Standard
The branch operates at the GLEUHR standard every day, with or without you in it. The walk-in patient at 6 pm receives the same care as the one at 9 am. The team holds the standard because they believe in it, not because they fear an inspection.
2.  Team
The team that ends the year with you is the team that started it — plus the new additions, minus the ones who outgrew the branch. Retention through warmth, development, fair correction, and visible leadership. The team that loves working here is the team that delivers.
3.  Brand
The patient who has a hard day in this branch leaves feeling owned — not defended against, not negotiated with. The brand reaches her even in the difficult moment, because you delivered it. The five-year client is built in those moments.
4.  Numbers
Conversion, retention, footfall, complaint rate — these all reflect upstream. If standard, team, and brand are held, the numbers follow. If the numbers are not following, something upstream is broken — do not chase the numbers, fix the upstream.
5.  Trust upward
HQ trusts you because you communicate cleanly, escalate well, never surprise them, and own your branch fully. The trust upward is what gives you the autonomy to run the branch the way it needs to be run.
13.  Quick Reference Card
Print this page. Keep it inside your desk drawer. Glance at it before the morning meeting with the doctor.
THE THREE AFFIRMATIONS  ·  TIMING
“Morning with the Doctor:  “We run this branch together. The patient gets the best of both.”    ·    The Escalated Complaint:  “This is mine to fix, not yours to chase.”    ·    The End-of-Day Close:  “Thank you, team. Today was good because each of you held your part.””

THE INNER STANCE  ·  RE-READ EVERY MORNING
“You are not the supervisor of this branch. You are the leader it reaches toward. Hold the standard, hold the team, hold the brand — in that order. Take responsibility by name when something has gone wrong. Name specifics in the close. The branch should run as well at 3 pm on your day off as at 11 am when you are in your chair.”

THE NEVER LIST  Never blame a team member in front of a patient. Never correct in public. Never decide a refund under pressure. Never let a patient walk out unowned. Never let HQ hear it from the patient before you. Never make a clinical decision — that is the doctor's. Never pick sides publicly. Never go home with a complaint undocumented. Never raise your voice on the floor.

Version 1.0   |   GLEUHR Branch Leadership
